title: Motion paths and bounce interpolation
content:
Part 1 keyframed the ball on every frame of the bounce. This part shows two quicker ways to get the same motion in Blender, using the same reference image: making the ball follow a motion path, and letting Bounce interpolation draw the bounces from just two keyframes.

Method 1: follow a motion path

  1. Fade the reference image. 0:00 Select the reference image and, in its Object Data properties, drag Opacity down so whatever you add on top stands out. Turn off its selection too (in the Outliner's Restriction Toggles, show Selectable and untick it) so you can't grab it by accident.

  2. Draw the path. 0:41 Press Shift+A and add a Curve → Bezier, rotate it 90° on Y, and move its start to the ball's first position. Press Tab for Edit Mode and drag the end point to the first contact with the ground, then turn its handle to match the curve.

  3. Add a point for each bounce. 1:22 Select the last point and press E to extrude a new one (click the middle mouse button to keep it in line). Repeat for each bounce. Press V and choose Free so the handles on either side of a contact can point different ways.

  4. Match the reference. 2:26 Adjust the handles until the curve sits on the reference's arcs. It doesn't have to be exact: the reference was drawn by hand.

  5. Add the ball and clamp it to the path. 3:06 Add a UV sphere, set its dimensions to 9 cm, and press Ctrl+A to apply the scale. In the Object Constraint properties, add Clamp To and pick the curve as its target.

  6. Keyframe the ball along the path. 3:47 On frame 1, move the ball along Y to the start of the curve, then right-click the Y location field and choose Insert Single Keyframe. Do the same on frame 31, then on the contact frames 25, 17 and 7, and on the tops of the bounces, frames 12 and 21. 4:28

  7. Smooth it in the Graph Editor. 5:10 Select every keyframe, press V and choose Free, then drag handles where the ball drifts off the reference. Check the in-between frames, add any you missed (frame 28 here 8:06), and play it back.

With a path, the ball can only move where the curve goes, so you only have to time it, not place it.

Method 2: Bounce interpolation

This one is quick but less flexible: Blender draws the bounces for you, so you get less control over their shape. 8:47

  1. Start a new ball. 9:29 Hide the first ball (H), add another sphere 9 cm across, and apply its scale.

  2. Keyframe the drop. 10:14 On frame 1, keyframe the ball's Z location at the top of the first arc. On frame 31, set Z to 0 and keyframe it.

  3. Make it bounce. In the Graph Editor, right-click and choose Interpolation Mode → Bounce. It works between any two keyframes.

  4. Move it across. 10:55 Keyframe Y on frame 1, then move the ball to the end position on frame 31 and keyframe Y again.

  5. Adjust the easing. 11:37 Drag the Y curve's handles to change how the ball speeds up and slows down. Turn on Normalize to compare the curves: the Z curve has the same shape as the path the ball takes.

Three ways to bounce a ball

12:50 Together with part 1, that's three ways to animate the bounce:

  • Keyframe every frame (part 1): the most control, and room for squash and stretch to give it character.
  • Follow a motion path: the path places the ball; you only time it.
  • Bounce interpolation: two keyframes and about two minutes of work, with the least control.
